newsitem.title: USA: CHESS-Kasparov fights to fool the computer Deep Blue.
newsitem.headline: CHESS-Kasparov fights to fool the computer Deep Blue.

text.p: Russian grandmaster Garry Kasparov, fighting to outwit the supercomputer Deep Blue in their re-match, chose a system of play in Wednesday's fourth game that is infrequently deployed at the top level.
World champion Kasparov surprised some expert observers with his decision because once again in the six-game match, he declined the temptation to play in his usual creative and attacking style.

"Garry has altered his style of play and how it has affected his ability to play is one of the questions we should be asking in this match," commentator and International Master Mike Valvo said. "It's not the Garry we see in tournaments against humans. He's allowing the computer to take the game to him."

Kasparov, 34, has failed to stamp his authority on the $1.1 million contest, although he won the first game on Saturday with finesse. He then resigned needlessly in Sunday's second game and was held to a draw in the third game on Tuesday despite having the advantage of the white pieces and the first move.
The match is tied at 1-1/2 points each. One point is awarded for a win and a 1/2 point for a draw. The winner over six games will collect $700,000 in prize money and the loser $400,000.

Kasparov, considered by most experts as the strongest player in chess history, defeated an earlier computer version over six games in Philadelphia in February 1996 with three wins, two draws and one loss

Playing with black pieces on Wednesday, Kasparov replied to Deep Blue's opening king's pawn move with the Prybl Defence or Czech opening that is named after Czech International Master Joseph Prybl, who specialises in the system.
The system is intended to reduce white's attacking options by careful piece placement and setting up a wall of pawns to defend the black camp.
"This position is not so easy for white to establish a clear path," U.S. grandmaster Yasser Seirawan said as the game progressed out of the opening into the middlegame.

Kasparov, who made a remarkable and rare miscalculation when he resigned the second game in a drawn position, was trying to stop the IBM computer from taking the lead in the match by forcing home its advantage of the white pieces.

The realisation that Kasparov had missed an opportunity to save the game on Sunday did not dawn on the chess world until well after the end of the game. The sequence of moves that would have led to a draw was discovered by an untitled player in the Internet Chess Club and confirmed by grandmasters in hours of intense analysis.

Deep Blue's programmers also said the computer had not evaluated the situation correctly, which prompted Kasparov to say that the machine was showing "signs of intelligence" and had made "a very human" decision.

The competition is part chess match and part scientific research project to help develop computers that can make complex, simultaneous calculations for applications such as weather forecasting, air traffic control and molecular dynamics.

Deep Blue is an IBM RS/6000 SP parallel processor with specialised microchips for chess. It can calculate hundreds of millions of moves per second and its software has been modified to include more chess knowledge.
The fifth and sixth games of the match were scheduled for Saturday and Sunday.
